title: 10 Neighborhoods, One Reason Each
description: Ten Roman areas, each anchored by one concrete feature—from ancient fragments and industrial structures to garden-city planning and film locations.

cards.title: Monti
cards.subtitle: For an unusually dense cross-section of ancient Rome.
cards.notes: The rione contains the Imperial Fora, Trajan’s Markets, the Domus Aurea and the Ludus Magnus—multiple archaeological layers within one central district.
cards.short_summary: Imperial sites are threaded through the neighborhood.

cards.title: Trastevere
cards.subtitle: For a Renaissance villa with rooms painted by Raphael and his school.
cards.notes: Villa Farnesina gives this riverbank rione a focused encounter with Renaissance architecture and fresco painting.
cards.short_summary: Villa Farnesina places Raphael’s frescoes inside the neighborhood.

cards.title: Testaccio
cards.subtitle: For a hill made from discarded Roman amphora fragments.
cards.notes: Monte Testaccio, or Monte dei Cocci, accumulated from transport vessels emptied near ancient Rome’s river port.
cards.short_summary: An ancient ceramic dump became the neighborhood’s defining landform.

cards.title: EUR
cards.subtitle: For a district planned around an exposition that never happened.
cards.notes: EUR was designed for the 1942 Roman Universal Exposition, canceled after the outbreak of World War II.
cards.short_summary: A canceled world exposition still shapes the district’s plan.

cards.title: Ostiense
cards.subtitle: For industrial infrastructure reused as part of the contemporary city.
cards.notes: The former Centrale Montemartini power plant now displays ancient Roman art as a Capitoline Museums venue.
cards.short_summary: A former power plant now holds classical sculpture.

cards.title: Garbatella
cards.subtitle: For streets and housing laid out on the garden-city model.
cards.notes: The neighborhood began in the 1920s with worker housing arranged in lots influenced by English garden cities.
cards.short_summary: Garden-city planning gives the area its small-scale urban form.

cards.title: Prati
cards.subtitle: For a Roman rione shaped by Piedmontese building styles.
cards.notes: Its post-unification development produced substantial Umbertine buildings alongside lighter Art Nouveau architecture.
cards.short_summary: Umbertine and Art Nouveau façades record Rome’s post-unification growth.

cards.title: San Lorenzo
cards.subtitle: For a public park dedicated to victims of the 1943 air raids.
cards.notes: Parco Caduti del 19 Luglio 1943 commemorates the people killed when bombing severely affected the neighborhood.
cards.short_summary: A neighborhood park holds the memory of the July 1943 bombing.

cards.title: Pigneto
cards.subtitle: For the streets where Pasolini staged much of Accattone.
cards.notes: The neighborhood’s connection to the 1961 film is still marked by several Pasolini-themed street artworks.
cards.short_summary: Pasolini’s Accattone remains legible in its streets and murals.

cards.title: Rione XVII Sallustiano
cards.subtitle: For the ancient garden complex visible below Piazza Sallustio.
cards.notes: Remains of the Horti Sallustiani survive about 14 metres beneath the modern street level.
cards.short_summary: Ancient garden architecture sits below the rione’s central square.
